en: The ability to make good judgments and quick decisions; sharp insight
hook: ACUMEN: ACUte MENtal sharpness.
story: Acumen. The ability to make good judgments and quick decisions; sharp insight. Monica's mother started with one sewing machine in a corner of their home. She noticed early that schoolgirls needed cheap, sturdy uniforms before every new term, so she stocked cloth months ahead. Ten years later she runs a workshop with twenty tailors. The neighbours call it luck, but Monica knows it is business acumen. Acumen comes from the Latin for sharpness, the same root as acute, so acumen is a sharp mind. So, what word names sharp judgment, especially in business? ... Acumen.

gre.s: Her political ____ was evident early: as a student organizer, she anticipated every move her rivals would make and outmaneuvered them all.
gre.clue: she anticipated every move her rivals would make

example: Her business acumen showed early, when at fifteen she turned her mother's pickle recipes into a small but profitable online shop in Khulna.

en: To confirm or support with additional evidence
bn: সমর্থন করা; প্রমাণ দিয়ে নিশ্চিত করা
hook: CO-ROBORATE: CO-ROBUST, makes a claim stronger with a partner's evidence.
story: Corroborate. To confirm or support with additional evidence. When a phone was stolen from the dorm common room, Tony told the warden he had seen a delivery man slip it into his bag. The warden was unsure. Then a second student came forward with the same story, and the security camera at the gate showed the man leaving in a hurry. Both corroborated Tony's account. The root robor comes from the Latin for strength, as in robust, so to corroborate is to strengthen a claim with support. So, what verb means to back up a claim with more evidence? ... Corroborate.

gre.s: The historian's theory remained speculative until newly discovered letters began to ____ it, confirming dates she had only inferred.
gre.clue: confirming dates she had only inferred

example: Satellite images corroborated the fishermen's account that the river had shifted nearly a kilometer east since the last survey.

en: A person's face or expression (noun); to tolerate or approve (verb)
hook: GRE trick: to COUNTENANCE means to tolerate — 'I won't countenance cheating.'
story: Countenance. A person's face or expression; as a verb, to tolerate or approve. Aiden's headmaster had a calm, kind countenance, and the students loved him. But when a boy was caught copying in the annual exam, that gentle face turned to stone. "I will not countenance cheating in my school," he said quietly, and the whole hall fell silent. On the GRE, watch for the verb: to countenance something is to tolerate it. Picture someone turning their face toward an act to approve it. So, what verb means to tolerate or allow? ... Countenance.

gre.s: The strict headmaster would not ____ even minor breaches of the dress code, sending students home for a missing tie.
gre.clue: sending students home for a missing tie

example: My grandfather, a retired schoolteacher, would never countenance lying, not even the small polite lies most families tell their guests.

en: Done quickly and without attention to detail
hook: CURSORY: like moving your CURSOR quickly down a page without reading.
story: Cursory. Done quickly and without attention to detail. Before signing the lease for his first flat, Isaac gave the contract only a cursory glance. He skimmed two pages, signed, and shook the landlord's hand. A month later he [sigh] discovered a clause making him pay for every repair in the building. Cursory comes from the Latin for running, like the cursor that runs across your screen, so a cursory reading runs over the page without stopping. So, what word describes a quick look that skips the details? ... Cursory.

gre.s: Because the inspector gave the bridge only a ____ examination, glancing at it from his car, the cracks in its supports went unnoticed.
gre.clue: glancing at it from his car

example: After only a cursory read of the contract, Arif signed it and later discovered a clause that doubled his rent after one year.

en: A shortage or lack of something
hook: DEARTH: DEAR because there's so little of it, like EARTH in a desert.
story: Dearth. A shortage or lack of something. In the dry months, a coastal village faces a dearth of fresh water, because salt has crept into its ponds and wells. Women like Martha walk an hour each way to fetch drinking water from a filter plant, carrying heavy pots on their hips. The dearth shapes every part of their day. Dearth comes from dear, in its old sense of costly: when something is scarce, it becomes dear. So, what word names a serious lack or shortage of something? ... Dearth.

gre.s: Given the ____ of reliable records from the period, historians must rely heavily on a handful of surviving letters.
gre.clue: must rely heavily on a handful of surviving letters

example: The dearth of qualified science teachers in rural upazilas means many students never watch a laboratory experiment performed in person.

en: Impartial; not influenced by personal advantage
hook: GRE trick: DISINTERESTED = no personal INTEREST (stake). Not the same as uninterested!
story: Disinterested. Impartial; not influenced by personal advantage. Two brothers in a river town were fighting over the family pond, and each wanted his own friend to judge the case. At last they agreed on Ruth, a retired judge from another district who knew neither of them and had nothing to gain. Her disinterested view settled the matter in one afternoon. Careful: disinterested means having no personal stake, while uninterested simply means bored. So, what word describes a judge with nothing to gain from either side? ... Disinterested.

gre.s: Because neither mediator had any financial stake in the outcome, both companies accepted them as ____ arbiters of the dispute.
gre.clue: had any financial stake in the outcome

example: The football federation asked a retired judge to lead the inquiry, hoping a disinterested outsider would settle the match-fixing rumors.

en: Asserting opinions as undeniably true, refusing to consider other views
hook: DOGMATIC: as stubborn as a DOG with a bone; sticks to DOGMA.
story: Dogmatic. Asserting opinions as undeniably true, refusing to consider other views. At every family dinner, Natalie's uncle insisted that only engineering and medicine were real careers. When Natalie said she wanted to study economics, he waved his hand without listening. When her cousin showed him salary figures, he simply repeated himself, louder. Natalie gave up. Her uncle was hopelessly dogmatic. A dogma is a belief accepted as beyond question, so a dogmatic person treats his own opinions as dogma. So, what word describes someone who insists he is right and refuses to listen? ... Dogmatic.

gre.s: Unlike his ____ colleagues, who refused to consider any evidence against their theory, the young professor welcomed criticism.
gre.clue: who refused to consider any evidence against their theory

example: My uncle is so dogmatic about politics that every family dinner ends with him lecturing the cousins and refusing to hear a reply.

en: One tier in a ranked structure, such as a company or society
hook: ECHELON: like the steps of a LADDER, rung by rung.
story: Echelon. One tier in a ranked structure, such as a company or society. Thirty years ago, Clark started as a tea boy in a downtown bank, carrying trays from floor to floor. He studied at night, passed exam after exam, and rose step by step. Today he sits in the highest echelon of the bank, on the top floor. He still [chuckle] makes his own tea. Echelon comes from the French for a rung of a ladder, so each echelon is one rung in a ranking. So, what word names a level or rank in an organisation? ... Echelon.

gre.s: Although she began as a junior typist, her talent eventually carried her to the highest ____ of the company, where she helped set policy for thousands of employees.
gre.clue: Although she began as a junior typist

example: Only the upper echelons of the civil service were invited to the briefing, so junior officers learned the news from television.

en: To come next, usually as a consequence of something
hook: ENSUE: follows like a SEQUEL.
story: Ensue. To come next, usually as a consequence of something. At a village wedding, someone set off a firecracker right behind the cows tied near the gate. Then [gasp] panic ensued. The cows broke loose, the guests scattered, and a pot of biryani tipped into the mud. In the chaos that ensued, the groom himself [laugh] ran after a calf in his wedding suit. Ensue comes from the same Latin root as sequel, so whatever ensues follows from what came before. So, what verb means to follow as a result? ... Ensue.

gre.s: When the dam's floodgates were opened without any warning, panic was bound to ____, and thousands of downstream residents fled their homes in the middle of the night.
gre.clue: thousands of downstream residents fled their homes

example: A long argument ensued when the umpire gave the batsman out, and play at the Mirpur stadium stopped for nearly ten minutes.

en: Former; previous
hook: ERSTWHILE: EARLIER, a while back.
story: Erstwhile. Former; previous. At a school reunion, Frank met his erstwhile best friend, Ronnie, for the first time in fifteen years. They had shared a bench in class eight and played cricket every afternoon, until Ronnie's family moved away. Now they were two grown men with grey hair, [laugh] trading the same old jokes. Erst is an old English word for earlier, so erstwhile means at an earlier while, once upon a time. So, what word describes someone who was your friend in the past? ... Erstwhile.

gre.s: The two nations, ____ enemies who had fought three wars in a single century, have since become close trading partners and allies.
gre.clue: have since become close trading partners and allies

example: The erstwhile jute mill on the riverbank now houses an art gallery, a cafe, and a rooftop basketball court.

en: A mild word substituted for one considered harsh or blunt
hook: EU-PHEMISM: EU = good, PHEME = speech. Good-sounding speech.
story: Euphemism. A mild word substituted for one considered harsh or blunt. When Tina's company cut forty jobs, the manager announced that the office was rightsizing. Nobody was fired; people were simply let go. Tina shook her head. Rightsizing was just a euphemism for sacking people, and let go was another euphemism. Eu means good in Greek, as in euphoria, and pheme means speech, so a euphemism is good-sounding speech for an ugly fact. So, what word names a soft, polite term used in place of a harsh one? ... Euphemism.

gre.s: Calling the mass layoffs a 'workforce optimization' was a transparent ____, a gentle phrase designed to disguise the harsh reality that thousands had lost their jobs.
gre.clue: a gentle phrase designed to disguise the harsh reality

example: The hospital's annual report used 'negative patient outcome' as a euphemism for death, which angered the families who read it.

en: To make a bad situation worse
hook: EXACERBATE: EXTRA ACID on a wound.
story: Exacerbate. To make a bad situation worse. Aaron had a small argument with his wife about money. Instead of apologising, he posted a joke about it on Facebook. Her sisters saw it. Her mother saw it. The small argument became a week of cold silence, and Aaron realised his joke had only exacerbated things. The root acerb comes from the Latin for bitter and harsh, as in acerbic, so to exacerbate is to make things even more bitter. So, what verb means to make a bad situation worse? ... Exacerbate.

gre.s: Rather than easing the shortage, the government's price controls only served to ____ it, as suppliers stopped selling at a loss.
gre.clue: Rather than easing the shortage

example: Cramming all night before the exam only exacerbated Sadia's headache, and by morning she could barely read the first question.

en: Nervous and muddled, especially after being surprised or rushed
hook: FLUSTERED: FLUSHED and FLUTTERED.
story: Flustered. Nervous and muddled, especially after being surprised or rushed. Sharon had practised her presentation all week. But the projector failed, the manager walked in early, and a phone rang loudly in the front row. Her cheeks went red, she dropped her notes, and she called the manager by the wrong name. She was completely flustered. Then she took a breath, [chuckle] smiled at herself, and started again. Flustered sounds like flushed and fluttered together: red cheeks and a fluttering mind. So, what word describes someone thrown into nervous confusion? ... Flustered.

gre.s: Though normally unflappable in debate, the senator became visibly ____ when a reporter produced the documents, stammering and contradicting his own earlier statements.
gre.clue: stammering and contradicting his own earlier statements

example: The usually calm news anchor looked flustered when the teleprompter froze halfway through her evening broadcast.

en: To abandon or give up entirely
hook: FOR-SAKE: abandon FOR your own SAKE.
story: Forsake. To abandon or give up entirely. Ralph grew up in the city and studied law, but when his father fell ill, he forsook his city career and went home to run the family tea garden in the hills. His friends thought he was mad. Twenty years later his tea is sold across the country, and he has never forsaken the workers who taught him the trade. Think of the old wedding vow, forsaking all others: to forsake is to give something up completely. So, what verb means to abandon something entirely? ... Forsake.

gre.s: Many of the reformer's early allies were quick to ____ her once her proposals became unpopular, leaving her to fight alone.
gre.clue: leaving her to fight alone

example: Rather than forsake his village, the doctor turned down a hospital post in Dhaka and kept running the small clinic his father had built.

en: A sign or person that announces something coming
hook: HARBINGER: a HERALD that announces what's coming.
story: Harbinger. A sign or person that announces something coming. In late winter, the first red blossoms of the silk cotton tree appear along the roads, and Joy's grandmother always says that spring is near. A few weeks later, the cuckoo begins to call from the mango trees. Both are harbingers of spring. Long ago, a harbinger was a messenger sent ahead of a king to find lodging, so a harbinger always arrives before what is coming. So, what word names a sign that announces something on its way? ... Harbinger.

gre.s: Many economists viewed the sudden collapse in housing prices as a ____ of the broader recession that would soon engulf the entire economy.
gre.clue: that would soon engulf the entire economy

example: For Dhaka students, the first kadam flowers on the campus trees are a cheerful harbinger of the monsoon.

en: Having a strong, exciting, intoxicating effect
hook: HEADY: goes straight to your HEAD.
story: Heady. Having a strong, exciting, intoxicating effect. When their team won the cricket match, Tyler and his friends ran into the streets with thousands of others, waving flags and banging pots until midnight. Strangers hugged, rickshaw pullers rang their bells, and car horns sang with joy. It was a heady night, and Tyler [laugh] did not sleep at all. Heady means it goes straight to your head, like a strong perfume or a great victory. So, what word describes an exciting feeling that goes straight to your head? ... Heady.

gre.s: For the young founders, the first months were ____: glowing press coverage and millions in investment arrived so quickly that they felt almost drunk with success.
gre.clue: felt almost drunk with success

example: Those were heady days for the young band, playing sold-out shows in three cities a week and hearing their song on every radio station.

en: Deliberate exaggeration for effect
hook: HYPER-BOLE: HYPER means over, too much. Over-the-top language.
story: Hyperbole. Deliberate exaggeration for effect. When Sid came home from his first day at a city coaching centre, he told his mother that the traffic was a hundred kilometres long, the classroom held a million students, and he had not eaten for a year. His mother [chuckle] simply handed him a plate of rice. She knew hyperbole when she heard it. Hyper means over and bole means throw, so hyperbole throws your words over the top. So, what word names exaggeration used for effect? ... Hyperbole.

gre.s: Although the critic called the film the worst ever made, her colleagues recognized the remark as ____ rather than a sober assessment.
gre.clue: rather than a sober assessment

example: When their father claimed he had walked a hundred miles to school as a boy, the children recognized the hyperbole and laughed.

en: To weaken or damage something
hook: IMPAIR: makes it IMPERFECT.
story: Impair. To weaken or damage something. Every winter, smoke from brick kilns around the city fills the air with a grey haze, and doctors warn that years of breathing it can impair children's lungs. When Rachel's little brother began coughing every night, the family bought an air purifier and kept the windows shut on the worst days. The smoke had already begun to impair his breathing. Impair comes from the Latin for worse, as in pejorative, so to impair is to make something worse. So, what verb means to weaken or damage, like smoke harming the lungs? ... Impair.

gre.s: Doctors warn that even moderate sleep deprivation can ____ judgment as severely as alcohol.
gre.clue: as severely as alcohol

example: Heavy lead exposure can impair a child's memory and concentration for years, long after the source has been removed.

en: Disturbing and horrifying because involving death or injury
hook: MACABRE: think 'MAKE A BURIAL' scene.
story: Macabre. Disturbing and horrifying because involving death or injury. During a power cut at his grandmother's village house, Zoe's cousin told a ghost story about a headless man who walked along the railway line at night, searching for his own head. The younger children [gasp] pulled the blanket over their faces. It was a macabre tale, full of graves and death. The word comes from the danse macabre, the dance of death painted on old European church walls, so a macabre story puts death at its centre. So, what word describes a grim story full of death and horror? ... Macabre.

gre.s: The museum's exhibit on the medieval plague was undeniably ____, displaying skulls, burial records, and paintings of corpses piled in the streets.
gre.clue: displaying skulls, burial records, and paintings of corpses piled in the streets

example: The novelist's macabre sense of humor shows in a chapter where a corpse is accidentally carried to the wrong funeral.

en: Wishing to do evil to others
hook: MALE-VOLENT: wishing (vol) BAD (mal).
story: Malevolent. Wishing to do evil to others. In the folk tales Shane's grandmother told, a demon often disguised herself as a beautiful queen, smiling sweetly at the king while secretly planning to eat his sons. Shane would grip his pillow every time she appeared. Her sweet smile hid a malevolent heart. Mal means bad and vol means wish, as in volunteer, so a malevolent person wishes harm on others. Its opposite is benevolent. So, what word describes someone who wishes evil on others? ... Malevolent.

gre.s: Far from being a neutral observer, the narrator is quietly ____, manipulating the other characters purely for the pleasure of watching them suffer.
gre.clue: purely for the pleasure of watching them suffer

example: Folk tales from the Sundarbans often feature a malevolent forest spirit who lures careless honey collectors deep into the mangroves.

en: Harmful, poisonous, or very unpleasant
hook: NOXIOUS: like NOX, toxic gas.
story: Noxious. Harmful, poisonous, or very unpleasant. Along the city river, tanneries and factories once poured their waste straight into the river, and a noxious smell hung over the black water. Boatmen like Jim wrapped cloth around their faces as they rowed. Fish disappeared, and children who swam there fell sick. Noxious comes from the Latin for harm, the same root as innocuous, which means harmless, so noxious is its opposite. So, what word describes fumes or waste that are poisonous and harmful? ... Noxious.

gre.s: The factory insisted its emissions were harmless, yet residents downwind reported headaches and nausea whenever the ____ fumes drifted over the town.
gre.clue: reported headaches and nausea

example: Burning plastic waste in open pits releases noxious smoke that settles over nearby rice fields and schoolyards.

en: Involving heavy, burdensome effort
hook: ONEROUS: a heavy ONUS (burden).
story: Onerous. Involving heavy, burdensome effort. When Rick became treasurer of his university club, he thought it would be easy. Instead he spent every night chasing receipts, counting coins, and arguing with seniors who never paid their dues. The job was so onerous that he lost five kilos in a month. When his term ended, he handed over the cash box with joy. Onerous comes from onus, the Latin for burden, so an onerous task sits on you like a heavy load. So, what word describes a duty that is heavy and burdensome? ... Onerous.

gre.s: Small businesses complained that the new regulations were so ____ that compliance alone would consume most of their profits.
gre.clue: compliance alone would consume most of their profits

example: Caring for three elderly relatives while working full time proved onerous, and Rokeya eventually hired a nurse for the afternoons.

en: Done with or employing great care and thoroughness
hook: PAINS-TAKING: TAKING great PAINS.
story: Painstaking. Done with or employing great care and thoroughness. In a small workshop in the old city, an old craftsman named Herbert restores broken clocks. He opens each one with tiny tools, cleans every gear with a soft brush, and sometimes spends a whole week on a single spring. His granddaughter Rose loves to watch him, holding her breath as he sets the last gear. Customers wait patiently, because his painstaking work never fails. Painstaking simply means taking pains, taking great trouble to get every detail right. So, what word describes work done with extreme care? ... Painstaking.

gre.s: The restoration was ____: over eleven years, a small team of conservators cleaned the enormous mural one square centimetre at a time.
gre.clue: one square centimetre at a time

example: Through painstaking interviews with hundreds of survivors, the researcher reconstructed daily life in a refugee camp in 1971.

en: Showy behavior meant to impress others or hide real intentions
hook: POSTURING: striking a POSTURE (pose) for show.
story: Posturing. Showy behaviour meant to impress others or hide real intentions. Before the local election, two candidates stood on stages across the road from each other, shouting promises, waving their fists, and calling each other cowards. Neither had a real plan. Old Ray, selling tea at the corner, [chuckle] shook his head. It was all posturing, he said, like two roosters puffing up their feathers. Posturing comes from posture: striking a pose for show. So, what word names showy behaviour meant only to impress? ... Posturing.

gre.s: Analysts dismissed the general's threats as mere ____, intended to impress his domestic audience rather than to signal any genuine intention of going to war.
gre.clue: intended to impress his domestic audience

example: Beneath all the posturing at the press conference, both boxers privately admitted that they respected each other enormously.

en: Spending money or resources recklessly and wastefully
hook: PRODIGAL son: the son in the parable who wasted his whole inheritance.
story: Prodigal. Spending money or resources recklessly and wastefully. When Nate's father sent him money for his university fees, Nate spent it in two months on a new phone, expensive restaurants, and gifts for friends he barely knew. When the fees were due, the account was empty, and his prodigal spree was over. He went home ashamed, and after a long silence his father forgave him. It echoes the parable of the prodigal son, who wasted his inheritance and then returned home. So, what word describes someone who wastes money recklessly? ... Prodigal.

gre.s: The government's ____ spending during the boom years left it with no reserves when the recession arrived.
gre.clue: left it with no reserves

example: A prodigal heir, Zaman spent his father's savings on imported cars within two years and then had to sell the family home in Dhanmondi.

en: Remarkably impressive in size, extent, or degree
hook: PRODIGIOUS: like a PRODIGY, extraordinary.
story: Prodigious. Remarkably impressive in size, extent, or degree. At a village fair, a farmer named Earl showed off a pumpkin so prodigious that it took three men to lift it onto the scale. Children [gasp] climbed onto carts to see it, and a photographer from the district newspaper came all the way from town. Prodigious shares a root with prodigy, a wonder or marvel, so anything prodigious makes people stare in wonder. So, what word describes something remarkably large or impressive? ... Prodigious.

gre.s: Mozart's output was ____: although he died at only thirty-five, he had already composed more than six hundred works.
gre.clue: more than six hundred works

example: Even as a child, the cricketer had a prodigious appetite for practice, batting for six hours a day in the lanes near his home.

en: A person who lives alone and avoids others
hook: RECLUSE: RE-CLOSED away from the world.
story: Recluse. A person who lives alone and avoids others. At the end of Nadia's lane stood a house with an overgrown garden and closed shutters. An old man lived there alone. He never came to weddings. Children called him a recluse and made up stories. Then Nadia learned he had once been a well-loved poet who chose silence after his wife died. Recluse comes from the Latin for shut away, so a recluse lives closed off from the world. So, what word names someone who lives alone, apart from others? ... Recluse.

gre.s: Though she was once the most celebrated socialite in the city, in her later years she became a ____, refusing all visitors and rarely leaving her house.
gre.clue: refusing all visitors and rarely leaving her house

example: After winning the prize, the poet became a recluse in a farmhouse near Kushtia, answering letters but refusing every interview.

en: Extremely distasteful; disgusting
hook: REPUGNANT: makes you REPEL and PUKE.
story: Repugnant. Extremely distasteful; disgusting. At a roadside restaurant on the coastal highway, Arnold found a cockroach floating in his dal. When he called the manager, the man simply scooped it out with a spoon and pushed the bowl back. Arnold [gasp] stared at him, then stood up and walked out. The whole place felt repugnant. Repugnant comes from the Latin for fighting back, as in pugnacious, so something repugnant makes your whole body fight against it. So, what word describes something so disgusting you want to push it away? ... Repugnant.

gre.s: Although a few found his argument intellectually intriguing, most readers considered the author's defense of slavery morally ____, an idea too abhorrent to be entertained.
gre.clue: an idea too abhorrent to be entertained

example: Many viewers found the advertisement repugnant because it used footage of starving children to sell luxury perfume.

en: Loyal, reliable, and hardworking
hook: STALWART: as STALL-WART, steady as a STALL that never moves.
story: Stalwart. Loyal, reliable, and hardworking. For forty years, Albert King has opened the village library at eight every morning, rain or shine. He dusts the shelves, mends torn books, and stays late when students need him. When floods closed the roads, he waded through knee-deep water with the keys. Everyone calls him a stalwart of the library. Stalwart comes from old English words for foundation and worth, so a stalwart is a person you can build on. So, what word describes someone loyal and utterly reliable? ... Stalwart.

gre.s: A ____ supporter of the union for three decades, she never wavered, even when other members abandoned it during the long and bitter strike.
gre.clue: she never wavered

example: A stalwart of the neighborhood library, Anwar Hossain has volunteered behind its desk every Friday for twenty-two years.

en: Equivalent in seriousness or effect to
hook: TANTAMOUNT: amounts to the same AMOUNT.
story: Tantamount. Equivalent in seriousness or effect to. During a mock GRE at a city centre, Marcus saw a classmate secretly photographing another student's answers. He told the invigilator. The classmate protested that he was only looking, but the invigilator said firmly that taking someone's answers was tantamount to stealing, and that staying silent would have been tantamount to helping. Tantamount comes from old French for amounting to as much, so if one thing is tantamount to another, they amount to the same. So, what word means equal in effect or seriousness? ... Tantamount.

gre.s: The senator argued that cutting the program's funding was ____ to abolishing it, since it could not operate on a smaller budget.
gre.clue: since it could not operate on a smaller budget

example: For a farmer, losing the irrigation pump in July is tantamount to losing the whole season's harvest.
